title: Start lean and price for real profit

say: Start lean, and price for real profit.
This is the video for module two of Introduction to Small Business and Trading.
Many women delay starting because they think they need a shop and a full stock. Most successful small businesses started much smaller. This is called a lean start.

say: Here is a worked example. Grace wants to sell soap, detergent, toothpaste and sanitary pads from a stall at her street junction in Port Harcourt.
Start-up money has three parts: equipment, first stock, and a cash reserve.

card.title: A lean start-up budget
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: Equipment: a wooden table, crates, an umbrella, a notebook and calculator. About 43,000 naira.

card.title: A lean start-up budget
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: First stock: 12 fast-moving items in small quantities, about 70,000 naira. Small amounts of many fast items teach her what customers really buy.

card.title: A lean start-up budget
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: Two weeks of running costs, transport, bags and the street levy, about 6,500 naira.

card.title: A lean start-up budget
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: And a cash reserve of about 20,000 naira for restocking and surprises.

card.title: A lean start-up budget
card.note: Naira figures are illustrative and approximate.

say: Total, 139,500 naira. Grace had planned to rent a shop at about 300,000 naira a year. Instead she opens at a stall, and will decide about a shop after six months of real sales.

say: Esther sells snacks and drinks in Abuja. She counts passers-by. At Spot A, in a quiet estate, about 40 people pass in 30 minutes. Rent is about 10,000 naira a month, and she expects about 8,000 naira in sales a day.

panel.heading: Esther compares two spots

say: At Spot B, beside a busy bus stop, about 150 pass. Rent is about 30,000 naira, but sales could reach about 30,000 naira a day. The extra rent is about 770 naira a day, far less than the extra sales. She chooses Spot B, and checks what levies apply.

panel.heading: Esther compares two spots

say: Kemi buys instant noodles by the carton in Lagos and sells single packs. One carton of 40 packs costs about 9,600 naira.

panel.heading: Find your true cost: Kemi's noodles

say: She buys 5 cartons and pays 2,000 naira for transport. That is 400 naira per carton.

panel.heading: Find your true cost: Kemi's noodles

say: So her landed cost per carton is 9,600 plus 400, which is 10,000 naira.

panel.heading: Find your true cost: Kemi's noodles

say: Divide by 40 packs. Her true cost is 250 naira a pack, not 240.

panel.heading: Find your true cost: Kemi's noodles

say: She sells at 300 naira, so gross profit is 50 naira a pack. Forgetting transport would have made her think she earns 60.

panel.heading: Find your true cost: Kemi's noodles
panel.rule: Landed cost = supplier price + transport + packaging.

say: Markup compares profit with what you paid. For Kemi, 50 divided by 250 is a 20 percent markup.

panel.heading: Same profit, measured two ways
items: Margin is always the smaller percentage

say: Margin compares profit with what the customer paid, so it is always the smaller percentage.
The danger is mixing them up. If you want a 30 percent margin but only add 30 percent to cost, you get less margin than you planned.

panel.heading: Same profit, measured two ways
items: Margin is always the smaller percentage

say: If you know the margin you want, use this formula. Selling price equals cost divided by 1 minus your target margin.
Ifeoma sells garri in buckets in Owerri. Her landed cost is about 2,400 naira.

panel.heading: Ifeoma prices a bucket of garri
panel.rule: Selling price = cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)

say: She wants a 25 percent margin. As a decimal, that is 0.25.

panel.heading: Ifeoma prices a bucket of garri
panel.rule: Selling price = cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)

say: 1 minus 0.25 is 0.75. And 2,400 divided by 0.75 is 3,200 naira. Her gross profit is 800 naira.

panel.heading: Ifeoma prices a bucket of garri
panel.rule: Selling price = cost ÷ (1 minus target margin)

say: Nearby sellers charge between 3,000 and 3,300 naira, so her price fits the market.
Remember, gross profit is not final profit. Rent, levies, bags and your own pay still come out of it. And when supplier prices rise, update your prices quickly.

say: Most small traders register a business name with the CAC, online through cac.gov.ng. Pay official fees only on the portal, and keep the account in your own name, because fake agents exist.
If you resell, check NAFDAC numbers and expiry dates, and never sell expired goods. If you make or package food or cosmetics, look into NAFDAC requirements. And keep receipts for every levy.

panel.heading: Registration and product safety
items: Most traders start with a CAC business name
Pay fees only on the official CAC portal
Resellers: check NAFDAC numbers and expiry

say: To remember. Budget for equipment, first stock and a cash reserve. Judge a spot by sales minus costs. Include transport in landed cost. Price from your target margin. Register when it helps you grow.
